subject: sg-succession
note: SPEC.md §8's declared pairing for sg-succession: the committed Intestate Succession Act corpus (left) against the 2026-08 cleanroom's encoding of the same Act (right). Written 2026-08-26 by the one role licensed to read both encodings; every measurement below was made against the tree on that date with the prebuilt l4 at dist-newstyle/build/aarch64-osx/ghc-9.10.3/jl4-0.1/x/l4/build/l4/l4.

SCOPE: THE ISA ONLY, and that is a limit of the comparator rather than a choice. `sides.<side>.module` is ONE module and `denovo-diff.mjs` refuses a `call` that the named module does not itself declare (imported rules are filtered out of the surface it reads back from `l4 render --include-unused`). This subject is FOUR Acts on each side — Wills, ISA, Probate and Administration, and (cleanroom only) Guardianship of Infants — so the Wills Act's formal-validity verdict and the Probate Act's grant machinery cannot be paired in the same map as the ISA's. They need their own maps, and the subject sidecar's `comparison.surface_map` holds exactly one path. Pointing the left at `sg-succession.l4` does not help: it re-exports the three Acts' decisions into scope but declares only eight rules of its own, so every ISA call would fail the same guard.

WHAT IS NOT COMPARED, AND WHY — THE DISTRIBUTION ITSELF. Not one of ISA s 7's nine rules is paired, and the reason is a compiler defect rather than a difference between the encodings. The cleanroom's survivorship turns on `family-domain.l4`'s `Vital status`, an enum (`living` / `died on HAS the date of death` / `dead, the date of death not known`); the comparator feeds every fact through `JSONDECODE`; and JSONDECODE cannot produce a constructor of an enum DECLARED AFTER A `§` SECTION HEADER. It falls through to the untyped decoder and yields a bare STRING, so the first `CONSIDER` over it raises `NonExhaustivePatterns`. Minimal repro, measured 2026-08-26: put `DECLARE `Vital status` IS ONE OF `living` …` above the first `§` in a file and `{"a0":"living"}` decodes; put the same DECLARE below a `§` and it does not. Records declared under a `§` decode fine, and a constructor CARRYING a payload (`died on`) cannot be fed under any arrangement — that half is a known limit of JSONDECODE, the section half is not. The consequence here: every cleanroom decision whose path reads `vital status` errors on every row — `section 5 — the person dies intestate after 2 June 1967`, `this Act has effect in respect of the estate`, `the distribution under rules 1 to 8`, `the persons entitled to succeed beneficially, and their shares` and everything under them. An error on one side and a value on the other reads as a divergence, which would be a harness artifact reported as a finding about the law; so those pairs are left out rather than written down. DENOVO-DIFF-ORACLE.md §8 states this limit in a stronger form than the tree now supports (`enum-typed input fields cannot be fed at all`); enums CAN be fed, but only nullary constructors, and only from a module with no `§` above them.

PAIRS CONSIDERED AND REJECTED, with the reason for each. (1) `the death falls within section 5` ~ `section 5 — the person dies intestate after 2 June 1967` — the right errors on every row through `Vital status`, above. (2) `the section 7 shares of` ~ `the distribution under rules 1 to 8` / `the persons entitled to succeed beneficially, and their shares` — same error, AND the results are not comparable as rendered: the left answers a LIST OF `Share` (taker, fraction, basis) and the right a LIST OF `Entitlement` (a `Person or corporation`, a fraction), so even repaired they would disagree textually on every row. The right's `the distribution, read out` is a LIST OF STRING and the left has no string-rendering decision to face it. (3) `the intestate distribution for` ~ `this Act has effect in respect of the estate` — the left's `Distribution` record could be projected on `governed by this Act` with `left.field`, and the two do ask the same question, but the right errors through `Vital status`. (4) `the Singapore immovable share of` ~ `the immovable property situated in Singapore, possessed beneficially` — REJECTED AS DISHONEST, not as broken: the left's is the net estate apportioned to the Singapore land (expenses and debts already off, rateably), the right's is the gross Singapore land less the property held as trustee, before any expense. They are two different quantities and pairing them would manufacture a divergence at every row. What actually turns on the difference is measured by `distributable-fund` instead. (5) `the proportion this Act governs in` ~ `section 10 — the part of his property not so disposed of` — the left answers a PROPORTION of the estate (0..1) and the right a MONEY amount; not the same question. (6) `section 6(a) — there shall be no distinction between those related through his father and those related through his mother` and `section 6(b) — those of the whole blood, the half blood ranking immediately after them` — present on the cleanroom side only. The committed corpus encodes s 6(a) in the SHAPE of its ontology (flat grandparent and uncle/aunt lists) and does not encode s 6(b) at all, so there is nothing to pair. Worth recording as an asymmetry: the committed `Family` cannot express a blood tie. (7) The Wills Act's formal-validity verdict (`the will is formally valid` ~ `the will is properly executed` / `s 6(1) — the will is in writing and executed in the manner mentioned in subsection (2)`) and the Probate Act's grant machinery — both look pairable and neither can live in THIS map; see the scope note above.

THE BATTERY IS HAND-WRITTEN. `battery.cases` is unset: the sg-succession sidecar declares no `legs['p7-dmn'].cases` file, so there is no DMN-sanitised seed set to un-sanitise. The 24 rows are built from the Act — s 2, s 4(1)-(2), s 5(a)-(b), s 7 rules 1-9, s 8, s 10 — and not from either encoding's fixtures; the fixture names in either module were not consulted for them.

PERTURBATION IS OFF BY CONSTRUCTION, AND THE REASON IS STRUCTURAL. `applyRename` in denovo-diff.mjs is TOP-LEVEL ONLY, so the union-payload technique that makes a row decode on both sides can align the four root fields and nothing deeper. Below that the two ontologies share exactly ONE field label — `name`, on the deceased — and they also disagree about DEPTH: the committed corpus puts `Muslim` and `domiciled in Singapore` inside `deceased`, the cleanroom puts `a Muslim` and `domiciled in Singapore at the time of his death` at the root of `Deceased person`. A single-field mutation of any such leaf therefore moves ONE side and leaves the other reading its own untouched twin, so the divergence it produces is a fact about this map and not about either encoding. Measured on this battery, 2026-08-26: with `enabled: true` the generator makes 24 seeds + 3,239 perturbations, and 3,237 of the 3,239 mutate a leaf that only ONE of the two records declares (computed from the two field lists `l4 render` reports, not sampled). The two exceptions are both `case.will.in writing`, the one shared label the generator can reach — and no live pair in this map reads the will, so even those two measure nothing. A confirming run truncated to 300 rows returned 136 divergences over 1,224 evaluations with 210 of 224 (pair, fact) leaves inert, and its two headline witnesses are the mirror pair that proves the mechanism: `case.deceased.Muslim` false->true gives corpus FALSE / cleanroom TRUE, and `case.a Muslim` false->true gives corpus TRUE / cleanroom FALSE. Neither is a fact about the Act. A one-sided mutation that reaches a paired decision manufactures a divergence; one that does not inflates the agreement count with a row in which nothing was measured. Both are worthless, so the instrument is switched off and the Sensitivity table in the report is EMPTY — the agreement figures below are UNWEIGHTED by leaf inertness, and two of the five pairs (`immovables-regulated`, `commencement`) are constant on both sides by the Act's own terms, so their agreement is a one-bit fact and not 24 independent ones. `slots.case.thresholds` is deliberately absent for the same reason: it feeds only the perturbation generator, and would be dead configuration here. The boundary work the generator would have done is done instead by rows written at the boundaries — the commencement date on 1, 2 and 3 June 1967, a nil estate, expenses exceeding the estate, and the trustee figure at, below and above the whole Singapore estate.

left.label: corpus
left.note: The committed hand corpus. Its nouns live in `sg-succession-domain.l4`, which `stageSide` picks up automatically because it sits in the same directory. `l4 render --include-unused` reports 27 non-imported rules and NO types for this module (they are all imported), which is why the comparator's every-declared-field check is inert on both sides here — a missing field would surface at evaluation as `Missing required field`, not at validation.

right.label: cleanroom

provenance.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 (2020 Rev Ed) (Singapore); see cleanroom-2026-08/source-bundle.json

right.note: The de novo encoding. 271 non-imported rules against the corpus's 27, over a shared ontology (`family-domain.l4`) that serves four Acts rather than three.

THE TYPE NAME CARRIES ITS OWN BACKTICKS, and it has to. `generateProbe` backticks the pair's `call` (the schema says so in terms) but emits the slot's `type` RAW into `a0 IS A <type>`, so a multi-word type name is lexed as two identifiers and the probe fails to typecheck with `The arities of the types do not match. I expected 0 arguments, but I found 1.` Writing the backticks in the map is the schema-conformant fix — it says the type is 'spelled exactly as it appears after IS A / IS AN', and in this module it appears with them — but a reader should know the alternative is a probe that will not compile. The regcf fixture never met this because all four of its slot types are single words.

note: ONE SLOT, because each side's decisions take one record: the corpus's `Case` and the cleanroom's `Deceased person`. The two root records line up field for field — `deceased`/`family`/`estate`/`will` against `the deceased`/`the family`/`the estate`/`the will` — and `rename` maps them.

EACH ROW IS A UNION PAYLOAD. Every object in `battery.rows` carries the field names BOTH ontologies declare, side by side: JSONDECODE ignores what the target record does not declare (measured — decoding `{"x":{"a":1,"b":2},"y":9}` into a record declaring only `x.a` yields the record cleanly), so each side reads its own vocabulary out of one object and the two sides are guaranteed to be looking at the same world. MAYBE fields may be omitted entirely: a missing MAYBE decodes to NOTHING.

SAME-NAME COLLISIONS WERE HUNTED FOR DELIBERATELY, because a leaf that both ontologies declare under ONE name with different types or different meanings is where the union technique fails silently. Across the four union records — `Deceased`∪`Person`, `Family`∪`Family`, `Estate`∪`Estate`, `Will`∪`Will` — the hunt found exactly TWO shared labels and NO collision of the dangerous kind. They are `name` on the deceased (left `Deceased`.`name` / right `Person`.`name`) and `in writing` on the will (left `Will`.`in writing` / right `Will`.`in writing`, both Wills Act s 6(1)). Both are benign: same L4 type, same statutory referent, one key that both sides read. `Case`∪`Deceased person`, `Family`∪`Family` and `Estate`∪`Estate` share no label at all. Two near-misses are worth naming because they are NOT collisions and read like them: the corpus's `funeral, testamentary and administration expenses` beside the cleanroom's `the funeral, testamentary and administration expenses`, and the corpus's `debts and liabilities` beside the cleanroom's `the debts and liabilities of the deceased`. Each pair differs by a leading article, so the two sides read two distinct keys; the battery writes the same figure into both. The corpus's `Family` and the cleanroom's `Family` share a type NAME and no field name at all. The corpus's `Will` and the cleanroom's `Will` likewise: `signed at the foot or end by the testator` against `signed at the foot or end thereof by the testator`, `expressed to be made in contemplation of that marriage` against `expressed to be made in contemplation of a marriage`.

WHAT THE UNION CANNOT REACH. Three facts sit at different DEPTHS and so appear twice under two keys: the Muslim gate (corpus `deceased.Muslim`, cleanroom root `a Muslim`), the domicile (corpus `deceased.domiciled in Singapore`, cleanroom root `domiciled in Singapore at the time of his death`) and the date of death (corpus `deceased.date of death`, cleanroom `deceased.vital status`, an enum the decoder cannot build). Every row states them consistently by hand; nothing in the harness enforces that, which is the other half of why perturbation is off.

The corpus's `family.children` and the cleanroom's `deceased.children` hold the same people in two shapes — a `LIST OF Person` against a `LIST OF Child`, each `Child` wrapping a `Person` with s 3's two legitimacy limbs. The battery states both, from the same facts.

rows.name: rule 2 and 3 — a surviving spouse and two surviving children
rule 4 — a surviving spouse, no issue, two surviving parents
rule 1 — a surviving spouse, no issue and no parent
rule 3 — issue only, one child predeceased leaving two of her own (per stirpes)
rows.note: ISA s 7 rule 3 Provisos (1)-(2). The stock of the predeceased child takes her share between them; the surviving child takes a whole share. This is where the two encodings' recursions are most likely to part company.

rows.name: rule 3 — every child predeceased, uneven stocks (fork F1's witness)
rows.note: Child A leaves two children, child B leaves one, both children predeceasing. The stirpital reading gives A's two a quarter each and B's one a half; the per capita reading gives all three a third. The committed corpus materialises this as fork F1.

rows.name: rule 6 — brothers and sisters, and the children of a deceased sister
rule 7 — two surviving grandparents and nobody nearer
rule 8 — uncles and aunts of the whole and the half blood
rows.note: ISA s 6(b) ranks the half blood immediately after the whole blood in the same degree. The committed ontology records no blood tie at all; the cleanroom's `Collateral relative` does.

rows.name: rule 9 — nobody within rules 1 to 8, so the Government takes
section 8 — two surviving wives and one child
rows.note: ISA s 8: the wives share between them the one share a single wife would have taken, so a second wife dilutes the wives and never the children.

rows.name: section 2 — the estate of a Muslim
rows.note: ISA s 2 takes the whole Act off the estate. Not a rounding error: the answer is a different body of law.

rows.name: section 5 — a death on 1967-06-01, the day before commencement
section 5 — a death on 1967-06-02, the day of commencement
section 5 — a death on 1967-06-03, the day after commencement
section 4 — domiciled abroad, both movable and immovable property in Singapore
rows.note: ISA s 4(2) reaches the Singapore land whatever the domicile; s 4(1) sends the movables to the law of the domicile.

rows.name: section 4 — domiciled abroad, only movable property in Singapore
section 4 — domiciled in Singapore, with property outside Singapore as well
rows.note: The committed ontology has no cell for property outside Singapore at all; the cleanroom has two. Neither s 5 limb reaches it, so the funds should still agree.

rows.name: section 5 — an estate with substantial debts
rows.note: The committed corpus takes the debts off the fund; the cleanroom takes only the expenses, and says in terms why the debts are not deducted.

rows.name: section 5 — expenses exceeding the whole Singapore estate
section 5 — part of the Singapore estate held as trustee and not beneficially
rows.note: "possessed beneficially" appears in both limbs of s 5 and again in its operative words. The cleanroom nets the trustee property out of the fund; the committed ontology has no cell for it at all. THE ROW STATES AN ASSUMPTION AND IT IS WORTH SEEING: the committed `immovable property in Singapore` and `movable property in Singapore` are written GROSS here, because with no trustee cell there is nowhere else for the trust property to go. A reader who takes the committed cells to mean the beneficial value already would say the row should carry trusteeSG = 0 on the cleanroom side too, and then the two agree. That choice is the divergence; it is not triaged here.

rows.name: section 5 — the whole Singapore estate held as trustee and not beneficially
rows.note: The far side of the previous row's boundary: the trustee figure now exceeds the whole Singapore estate, so s 5's own gate closes on the cleanroom side (neither limb is made out) and its fund is nil. Same stated assumption; see the previous row.

rows.name: section 5 — a nil Singapore estate
section 10 — a will beneficially disposing of part of the property
rows.note: The committed corpus records the undisposed part as a PROPORTION of value; the cleanroom computes it from the will's own dispositions. Neither of the live pairs reads the will, so this row exercises the union payload's will branch and nothing else.

rows.name: section 10 — a will beneficially disposing of the whole of the property

perturbation.note: Off by construction — see the map-level note. Turning it on does not measure the two encodings; it measures the union payload.

battery.note: 24 rows, in the corpus's field vocabulary plus the cleanroom-only keys the rename cannot reach. No `cases` file: the sg-succession sidecar declares no p7-dmn cases.

left.call: the Act applies to the estate of

right.call: this Act applies to the estate

pairs.note: The hardest gate in the Act: it does not shade the answer, it removes the Act. Both sides encode s 2 as a single already-construed fact about the deceased, and both take the section's converse as the gate every operative rule reads — the corpus by negating `Muslim` in place, the cleanroom by naming the exclusion (`section 2 — nothing in this Act applies to the estate`) and deriving the application from it. Note that the corpus's `note` on refusal names the Administration of Muslim Law Act 1966 while the cleanroom's own comment refuses to name any statute, on the ground that s 2's text names none; that difference is in prose, not in an answer, so this pair cannot see it.

left.call: this Act regulates the movables of

right.call: section 4(1) — the law of the country of domicile is the law of Singapore

pairs.note: s 4(1) sends movables to the law of the domicile, so 'this Act regulates them' is 'the domicile is Singapore'. Both sides reduce the section to that one boolean and both record, in prose, that the section really asks WHICH country and that the binary cannot answer what governs when the answer is not Singapore.

left.call: this Act regulates the Singapore immovables of

right.call: section 4(2) — the distribution of the immovable property is regulated by this Act

pairs.note: CONSTANT ON BOTH SIDES, and that is the finding: s 4(2) has no antecedent — 'wherever he may have been domiciled' is the point of it — and both encodings render it as an unconditional TRUE. A de novo encoder could plausibly have made it conditional on domicile, or folded it into s 5; neither did. The arities differ (the corpus threads a `Case` it does not read, the cleanroom takes nothing), which the schema allows on purpose. Because both answers are constant, 24 rows of agreement here are one bit of evidence, not 24.

CONSTANT ON BOTH SIDES: both name the commencement 2 June 1967 and both build it with `YMD`. One bit of evidence, and a real one — the date is the kind of fact a de novo reading transcribes wrongly. Note what this pair does NOT measure: whether the two agree that the section is satisfied by a death ON that day. Both encode s 5's 'after 2 June 1967' with a strict GREATER THAN, but the decisions that apply it (`the death falls within section 5` ~ `section 5 — the person dies intestate after 2 June 1967`) cannot be paired, because the cleanroom's reads `Vital status`. The battery still carries the 1, 2 and 3 June rows so that the day this is repairable the boundary is already written down.

left.call: the property this Act distributes in

right.call: section 5 — the property to be distributed, after payment thereout of the expenses of due administration

note: THE ONE SUBSTANTIVE PAIR IN THIS MAP, and the only one that discriminates over more than two values. Both decisions answer s 5's question — the value this Act distributes, as against the whole estate — and both are the quantity every share the Act computes is a fraction of. The corpus says so at its definition ('The value this Act actually distributes, as opposed to the whole estate'); the cleanroom says so at its ('Every fraction in s 7 is a fraction of this, not of the gross estate').

The cleanroom's fork register carries this ground twice over: F-ISA-A7 is the fund and its floor, F-ISA-A6 is 'possessed beneficially', F-ISA-A17 is which cell the trustee figure comes off. The committed corpus's own register carries F5 against `the Singapore immovable share of` — the rateable-expenses reading — which is the other half of the same disagreement. Both registers are cited here rather than one, because `pair.fork` takes a single id.
NOT TRIAGED, and deliberately not: which side is right about the debts, about the floor, and about property held on trust is a reading of ISA s 5 and belongs to a human.
